title: My diet for Natural Hypertrophy
summary: NH describes his own diet: mostly vegetables by volume, plus chicken, fish (limited fatty fish), up to a pound of red meat a week, few eggs, goat cheese, water, and snacks like cashews, olives and sardines, shaped by a hereditary disease he must prevent. He doesn't track calories (estimates 2200-2400 kcal), eats two big meals, is recomping by following hunger, and stresses that diet is individual and anti-dogmatic, though most people benefit from vegetables, whole foods and home cooking.

claims.claim: Diet is like training: you must learn how your own body works; borrow ideas from others but check they fit you.
He is suspicious of any diet advice claimed to work for 100% of people; general rules cover most people but always need individual tweaks.
He trained for sports, then strength, now size and aesthetics, and always built effective training without reading books, making up for mistakes with hard work.
Being stubborn with diet is more detrimental than being stubborn with training; hard work compensates less.
Novices who aren't already over- or underweight can basically eat whatever and just increase quantities; food quality starts mattering later. He still recommends whole foods and cooking.
He calls himself plant-based in the old sense: the bulk of his diet by volume is vegetables, mostly greens and colorful vegetables, with limited rice and potatoes; he is not vegan.
He has a hereditary disease risk and uses diet as the main way to prevent it, which shapes many of his restrictions.
His staples: spinach, cabbage, green onions, lots of onions and garlic, peppers of every color, citrus (cuties, oranges, limes), asparagus and Brussels sprouts.
Don't eat 'bodybuilding' or 'healthy' foods that don't agree with you: broccoli wrecks his stomach so he skips it; people who can't digest raw spinach should stop eating it.
Veganism benefits many people but isn't the easy fad it became and doesn't suit everyone, e.g. those in climates with no winter harvest; some people need animal products to be healthy.
He eats animal products because he likes them, they kill his hunger and suit his body: lots of chicken, fish (likes salmon, eats much tilapia).
Because of his condition he must keep omega-3 levels from getting too high, so he limits fatty fish and fish oil.
Red meat is bad for him specifically (not everyone; he knows people eating pounds weekly who live long), so he limits himself to 1 lb of red meat per week and avoids overcooking it.
He likes goat cheese, avoids milk because it's bad for him, and drinks mostly water, in large amounts.
His snacks: cashews, green olives, sardines. He eats the same foods day in, day out.
He eats 4-8 eggs a week now, down from 12 a day in the past, for health reasons.
He cooks everything himself, preferably in the oven, and avoids microwave ready-meals.
By volume his diet is mostly low-calorie, micronutrient-rich vegetables, but calories come largely from animal products; he usually has animal products in one meal, reducing portions if in both.
He eats two big sit-down meals a day plus snacks or a breakfast between.
He'd be described as having a 'low metabolism' and does fine on relatively few calories.
He doesn't count calories or macros and high-balls everything, because he is already obsessive about training and weighing food would make him go crazy.
Part of why he won't take PEDs is that the tracking involved would damage his mental health.
He estimates he eats around 2200-2400 kcal a day.
He doubts the accuracy of smaller lifters claiming to eat 4000 kcal a day; either they miscount or they overfeed.
His meals are cheap and easy; good food isn't hard to make.
He is currently recomping at stable bodyweight simply by following his hunger.
He doesn't weigh himself; he judges progress by strength and the mirror.
When he is in a caloric deficit and losing weight his strength drops immediately with no warning, so getting stronger tells him he isn't losing weight.
Most people would benefit from eating mostly vegetables complemented by animal products, eating whole foods, and cooking themselves rather than buying microwave meals; it's also cheaper.
Diet is case by case; people who say everyone should eat only raw meat or only vegetables are too dogmatic.
